scenes.title: max_tokens is an exam's word limit, with a strict invigilator
scenes.body: When time is up, the invigilator **takes the paper mid-sentence**. The model doesn't plan its answer to fit `max_tokens`; it is simply **stopped**. `stop_reason` tells you if that happened.

scenes.body: Without streaming, you **download the whole movie** before pressing play. With streaming, it **starts playing in seconds** while the rest arrives. Same total data, a much better wait.

scenes.title: Structured output is a government form, not a letter
scenes.body: A letter can say anything, in any order. A form has **fixed boxes**: name here, date there. A program can read a form without guessing. Structured outputs make the model fill in a form.

scenes.title: Refusals: check before you read
scenes.body: If `stop_reason` is `"refusal"`, the model declined and the content may be empty. Check it **before** reading the text. The API can also retry a declined request on another model automatically (`fallbacks`), which our project turns on.

items.q: Why would you stream an LLM response?
items.a: Generation happens token by token, so streaming shows text **as it is produced**: the user sees progress in moments, total time is the same, and very long replies avoid request timeouts.
items.trap: Saying streaming makes the model faster. It doesn't; it makes the wait feel shorter.

items.q: How do you get reliable JSON from an LLM?
items.a: Use **structured outputs**: pass a JSON schema (or a Pydantic model) so the reply is constrained to it, parse into an object, and still check `stop_reason` and validate business rules.
items.trap: "Ask for JSON in the prompt and fix it with regex." That breaks on the first unusual reply.
